text: Invasive breast carcinoma of no special type (invasive ductal carcinoma) shows malignant epithelial cells infiltrating the stroma in nests, cords, and tubules, and is the most common invasive breast cancer.
Invasive lobular carcinoma classically grows as single-file cords of small, discohesive cells infiltrating the stroma, often in a targetoid pattern around residual ducts.
Loss of membranous E-cadherin expression is characteristic of invasive lobular carcinoma and reflects the discohesive growth caused by CDH1 inactivation, distinguishing it from ductal carcinoma.
Ductal carcinoma in situ is a non-invasive proliferation of malignant epithelial cells confined within the ductal-lobular system by an intact myoepithelial layer and basement membrane.

Invasive breast carcinomas are graded by the Nottingham system, summing scores for tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism, and mitotic count; high nuclear grade tumours show marked pleomorphism and brisk mitoses.
Benign breast tissue and fibrocystic change retain organised ducts and lobules with a preserved two-cell layer (epithelial plus outer myoepithelial cells) and no stromal invasion.

The Nottingham grading system is the modified Scarff-Bloom-Richardson method; the three component scores (each 1 to 3) are added, with a total of 3 to 5 giving grade 1, 6 to 7 grade 2, and 8 to 9 grade 3.
The tubule formation score reflects the proportion of tumour forming glandular or tubular structures with central lumina: more than 75% scores 1, 10 to 75% scores 2, and less than 10% scores 3.

The nuclear pleomorphism score grades increasing variation in nuclear size, shape, and chromatin: small uniform nuclei score 1, moderate variation scores 2, and marked pleomorphism with prominent nucleoli scores 3.

The mitotic count score is based on the number of mitotic figures per 10 high-power fields calibrated to the microscope field area, with more mitoses giving a higher score and indicating more aggressive tumour proliferation.

Lobular carcinoma in situ is a non-invasive proliferation of small, discohesive cells filling and distending the acini of a lobule, typically with loss of E-cadherin and considered a risk factor and non-obligate precursor of invasive carcinoma.

Normal breast parenchyma is organised into terminal ductal-lobular units, where each lobule and duct is lined by an inner luminal epithelial layer and an outer myoepithelial layer resting on an intact basement membrane.
